segments.say: Let's slow everything down now. You've listened for a long time, and there's nothing left to do, so let yourself settle into wherever you are, and let your breathing find its own gentle pace.

There's nothing to do right now. Nothing to remember, nothing to write down, and nothing to decide. If your mind has wandered off at any point during the evening, that's perfectly fine, because wandering is something minds do, and we've spent the whole time learning that it's a useful thing.

Let your shoulders drop, just a little. Let your jaw loosen, and your hands rest wherever they are. Feel the weight of your body being held up by the bed or the chair, so that you don't have to hold yourself up at all. All of that work can stop for now.

Take a slow breath in, and let it out even more slowly. There's no need to count, and no need to do it perfectly. Just let the breath go out like a tide, and let the next one arrive by itself. Each breath is a small, quiet moment with nothing in it that needs fixing.

Think of an empty moment, the kind we spent the evening studying. Only this time, it isn't an itch, and it isn't a problem. It's simply a pause, a space between one thing and another, with no one asking anything of you. It can be quiet, and warm, and perfectly enough.

A still harbour at the edge of evening, with small boats resting on glassy water and a few windows glowing warmly along the shore. The sky above is soft violet, the light is fading slowly, and everything seems to be settling in for the night.

Time, which we saw can stretch and shrink, is allowed to go as slowly as it likes. There's no clock that needs watching tonight. If the minutes feel long, they're only long and soft. If they pass quickly, you'll hardly notice. Either way, there's nowhere you need to be.

If a thought comes, let it come. It might be about tomorrow, or about something from long ago, or about nothing in particular. You don't have to follow it, and you don't have to push it away. Let it drift past, like a boat across a quiet harbour, and watch it go.

If you feel a little curious about something, that's all right too. A small, soft wondering, about the sound of rain, or the colour of the dark, or the way a room feels at night. Curiosity, at this hour, needn't ask for an answer. It can simply be there, like a candle in a window.

Let's be kind to ourselves, for these few minutes. Kind to the part of us that gets restless, and kind to the part that wants to do something with every spare moment. Both of them are trying to look after us, in their own ways, and both can rest for now.

Somewhere, in an imagined room, a woman called Mira is sitting by a window with a cup of tea, looking out at a garden getting dark. Her phone is charging in another room. She has no idea that she has been the guide to a long evening, and she wouldn't mind. She's watching the light go.

The quiet around you is wide and soft. It isn't empty, though. It's full of small, gentle things. The hum of a house, the distant sound of a car, the faint rhythm of your own breath. Let all of it be background, like a slow tide, going in and out at its own pace.

You're allowed to do nothing. You're allowed to rest without having earned it. You're allowed to have a pause in which nothing is achieved, and nothing is learned, and nothing is improved. That's not wasted time. That's just time, resting.

Let yourself notice the room around you, without opening your eyes, if they're closed. The air is the temperature it needs to be. The sounds outside are far away, and they aren't asking for anything. The bed, the blanket and the pillow are doing their quiet work, and for the moment, there's nothing else that needs doing.

Think of boredom, and curiosity, and rest, as a kind of tide. They come in, and they go out, and none of them stays forever. You don't have to pull any of them in, or push any of them away. They return on their own, as they always have, from the desert cells to the waiting rooms of today.

Let your hands become heavy, and warm, and loose. The fingers don't have to hold anything, or reach for anything, or press anything. They can simply rest, the way they would if you were already half asleep. All that reaching we talked about, for pockets, for screens and for snacks, can be put down for now.

Imagine your mind as a wide, slow sky at the end of a long day. Thoughts are small clouds, drifting across it at their own pace. Some are bright, and some are grey, and none of them needs a name. The sky doesn't try to hold any cloud, and it doesn't try to push one away. It just stays open.

Outside, the evening is doing what evenings do. The light is fading, the streets are quietening, and windows are glowing here and there in the dusk. Inside, wherever you are, there's a small pocket of warmth that belongs to you. It doesn't need to be anything more than that.

Many of the best moments in life sit in the pause between two things. The pause between a day and a night, between an out-breath and an in-breath, between a question and its answer. Boredom lives there too, and so does curiosity, and so does rest. Tonight, the pause is just a pause, and it's perfectly gentle.

With each breath, let yourself sink a little further into the quiet. Heavier, warmer, slower. The ideas of the evening can drift away now, one by one, like leaves on a slow stream, leaving only the stillness they were floating on.

If there's one last thing to think about, let it be small and kind. Something that went a little better than expected today, or something you're looking forward to, however tiny. And then let that thought go too, and let the quiet take its place, deep, warm and unhurried, with nowhere left to go.

So, from here, there's only one thing left to say. Thank you for spending this long evening with us, for your curiosity and your patience. Be gentle with yourself tonight, and tomorrow. Rest well, or sleep well, and we'll see you next time.
Next time, we'll look at one of the strangest feelings the mind can produce, that sudden, eerie sense of having lived this exact moment before, and ask what scientists think is really going on.
